reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard sleep & reproductive medicine references
clinicalPearls: Infertility is conventionally defined as failure to conceive after twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse, with earlier evaluation warranted for women over thirty-five or with known risk factors
Female causes fall into ovulatory, tubal/pelvic, and uterine/cervical categories, and both partners should always be assessed together
Ovulatory dysfunction is a leading cause, with polycystic ovary syndrome the commonest example, alongside hypothalamic, pituitary, and premature ovarian insufficiency causes
Ovarian reserve declines with age, and this age-related fall in oocyte quantity and quality is the single most important prognostic factor
Confirming ovulation, assessing tubal patency, and evaluating the uterine cavity form the core diagnostic framework
Tubal damage from prior pelvic infection, endometriosis, or surgery is an important and sometimes silent cause
Reversible lifestyle contributors such as extremes of body weight, smoking, and excess alcohol should be identified and addressed
Management ranges from ovulation induction and correction of anatomical problems to assisted reproductive techniques, chosen according to the underlying cause and ovarian reserve
reference.pathophysiology: Female fertility requires cyclical hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian function producing a mature oocyte, patent fallopian tubes to allow fertilisation and transport, and a receptive endometrial cavity for implantation. Ovulatory disorders arise from disrupted gonadotrophin secretion: hypothalamic causes (stress, low body weight, excessive exercise, hyperprolactinaemia), polycystic ovary syndrome with anovulation, or premature ovarian insufficiency with follicular depletion. Tubal and peritoneal factors result from scarring and adhesions after pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, or surgery, impairing gamete transport. Uterine factors include fibroids distorting the cavity, intrauterine adhesions, and congenital anomalies that impair implantation. Advancing maternal age reduces both the number and chromosomal quality of remaining oocytes, lowering fecundity and raising miscarriage risk.
additionalDifferentials: Hypothalamic amenorrhoea from weight, stress, or exercise
Tubal factor from previous pelvic inflammatory disease or surgery
Uterine fibroids, polyps, or intrauterine adhesions
additionalInvestigations: Confirmation of ovulation using cycle history and mid-luteal progesterone
Assessment of ovarian reserve with relevant hormonal markers and antral follicle count
Tubal patency evaluation by hysterosalpingography or laparoscopy
Pelvic ultrasound and, where indicated, hysteroscopy to assess the uterine cavity
Thyroid function and prolactin measurement, plus partner semen analysis
redFlags: Amenorrhoea with elevated gonadotrophins in a young woman indicating premature ovarian insufficiency
Symptoms or signs of a pituitary tumour with hyperprolactinaemia
Severe pelvic pain or an adnexal mass requiring urgent gynaecological assessment
Advancing maternal age prompting timely rather than delayed investigation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on the cause and on ovarian reserve; ovulatory disorders often respond well to induction of ovulation, whereas outcomes decline with maternal age and reduced reserve, and assisted reproduction can help many but not all couples.
pitfalls: Delaying investigation in older women where declining ovarian reserve makes time critical
Assessing only the female partner and omitting semen analysis
Overlooking silent tubal disease from past infection or endometriosis
Failing to address modifiable factors such as weight, smoking, and alcohol before intervention
management: Optimise modifiable factors including healthy body weight, smoking cessation, reduced alcohol, folic acid supplementation and correction of hypothalamic causes such as excessive exercise or low body weight
Induce ovulation in anovulatory disorders such as polycystic ovary syndrome with agents like letrozole or clomifene, adding gonadotrophins where these fail
Treat identified endocrine causes with dopamine agonists for hyperprolactinaemia and correction of thyroid dysfunction
Undertake surgical management of tubal, uterine or pelvic factors including tubal surgery, hysteroscopic division of adhesions or removal of submucosal fibroids, and treatment of endometriosis
Offer assisted reproductive technology, particularly in-vitro fertilisation, for tubal disease, reduced ovarian reserve, advancing maternal age or failure of simpler measures
Assess and treat the male partner concurrently and counsel on the strong prognostic impact of maternal age and ovarian reserve
Refer to reproductive medicine specialists and consider donor oocytes or fertility preservation where ovarian reserve is severely reduced
